notes: 499 initially admitted to hospitals in Moscow and Kiev for observation on night of 26 April 1986 and days after
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D p.58; Chernobyl Forum 2005

notes: 237 emergency workers initially examined for ARS signs; preliminary clinical assessment
134 confirmed ARS after dosimetric and clinical review; 103 downgraded; range 0.8-16 Gy whole body dose; emergency workers and first responders
Grade I (mild): 140 patients; doses roughly 0.8-2 Gy; bone marrow suppression; nausea vomiting; full recovery expected; no deaths in this group
Grade II (moderate): 55 patients; doses ~2-4 Gy; haematopoietic syndrome; significant bone marrow depression; 1 death; most survived
Grade III (severe): 21 patients; doses ~4-6 Gy; severe bone marrow failure plus radiation skin burns; 7 deaths; required BMT in some cases
Grade IV (very severe): 21 patients; doses ~6-16 Gy; GI syndrome + bone marrow destruction + severe radiation burns; 20 deaths; only 1 survivor in this group; skin doses 400-500 Gy on some patients
2 immediate deaths on night of accident: Valery Khodemchuk (steam explosion) and Vladimir Shashenok (acute injuries from steam/explosion at 01:23 26 April 1986)
28 confirmed ARS deaths within 3 months (April-July 1986); predominantly Grade III-IV; causes: bone marrow failure + skin burns + GI syndrome
28 ARS deaths + additional early deaths = ~31 in first weeks; OECD-NEA Ch.V specifies "31 deaths in first weeks"
ARS survivors subsequent deaths: 11 by 2000 (UNSCEAR 2000); 8 more died 2000-2006 = 19 total survivor deaths through 2006; causes not all radiation-related
13 bone marrow transplants performed; only 2 engraftments; 11 of 13 BMT patients died; concurrent radiation skin burns reduced effectiveness of BMT; BMT had limited impact on outcome

Skin doses exceeded bone marrow doses by factor 10-30; many ARS patients received skin doses 400-500 Gy; radiation burns to skin were major contributor to at least 19 of deaths; burns >50% body surface area led to major infections
Many patients who suffered moderate-severe ARS developed radiation-induced cataracts in first few years; strong correlation between ARS grade and cataract prevalence
Over the years increase in haematological malignancies in ARS survivors; haematopoietic recovery substantial in many patients; significant local skin injuries remain
No ARS cases among general public evacuated or non-evacuated; consistent with dose assessment showing whole-body doses far below ARS threshold (~700 mGy) in all civilian populations
Dr. Angelina Gus'kova led treatment at Moscow Hospital No.6; pioneered diagnosis and management of radiation-induced ARS; significant advance in nuclear medicine understanding
Reactor operators on duty at 01:23 and first responder firefighters received highest doses ~8-16 Gy; all died; exact doses reconstructed retrospectively as no badges survived or were saturated
Gastrointestinal syndrome (GI tract damage) in 15 patients; radiation pneumonitis in 8 patients; complicating bone marrow syndrome in highest-dose group
Total definite deaths attributed to accident: 2 immediate (explosion/burns) + 28 ARS = 30; some sources cite 31 with different attribution; CNSC Canada cites 2+28=30
